dimension_grades.evidence: The Redis connection pool theory is described in full detail: reading ioredis source code, finding a closed 2021 issue, writing a test harness, simulating thousands of connections — all for nothing over a day and a half.
'The real bug — the one that cost us three and a half extra days — was me, choosing investigation theater over the boring diagnostic step that would have actually worked.'
'By Tuesday afternoon — a full day and a half in — I was still staring at Redis internals' and 'The whole thing took four days. It should have taken four hours.'
'I'd been doing the engineering equivalent of diagnosing a car engine by reading the owner's manual in a different room from the car' — wry and self-deprecating without being self-pitying.
The author shows initial misreadings: 'No caching layer. No in-memory store. At least, not one I remembered writing' and 'I grep'd the codebase... I found nothing suspicious. Our code was clean.'
Clues build incrementally: heap snapshot → object shape identified → retainer chain traced → Map in module scope → node_modules → specific library → specific cache key line.
The root cause (the unbounded Map in fast-schema-check) only appears after the Redis dead end, the grep that found nothing, and the retainer chain trace — sustained over multiple sections.

'I felt that little dopamine hit of I've found it' (false hope), 'I heard how thin it sounded' (embarrassment), and 'I watched it for an hour, refreshing the dashboard like a nervous parent' (relief).
Each takeaway names a specific behavior: heap snapshot before forming any theory (made a checklist item in runbook), search node_modules early, explain hypothesis out loud before investing two hours.
'I'm not going to tell you to always monitor your memory or profile before optimizing. You know that. I knew that. I did it anyway.'

Each takeaway references a specific narrative moment: the snapshot rule ties to 'The snapshot on Tuesday would have saved me a full day if I'd taken it on Friday'; the out-loud rule ties to Priya's question in standup.
'You know that. I knew that. I did it anyway' treats the reader as an equal who already knows the basics rather than someone being instructed.
Only two code snippets appear in the entire post — the library's validator.js and the before/after usage fix — both directly serving the narrative.
The critical line in the first snippet is marked '// <-- THIS LINE' and the second snippet has '// disable internal cache' and '// Before:' / '// After:' comments.
The fix section explicitly shows 'Before: default caching behavior (unbounded Map)' and 'After: caching disabled' with both code versions presented.
'I opened the relevant file and found this:' followed by 'Look at that cache key' directs the reader's attention before and after the snippet.
The opening scene includes '4:47 PM on a Friday,' the Datadog sawtooth pattern description, RSS at 1.2 GB on a 1.5 GB container, and the PagerDuty notification lighting up the phone.
Real tool names used throughout: PagerDuty, Datadog, Jira, Kubernetes, Chrome DevTools, Kafka, Postgres, ioredis, ajv, fast-schema-check, Slack.

The Wednesday morning grep section and the retainer chain discovery are narrated in retrospective summary ('I grep'd the codebase... I found nothing') rather than dramatized as live scenes with action and immediacy.
